text: Coverage centres on the Casalinho da Ajuda social-housing enclave, which press reports place among Lisbon's flagged "zonas vermelhas" drug neighbourhoods; in November 2022 CNN Portugal reported the PSP cordoning off the bairro after a string of stoning attacks on Carris buses. Correio da Manhã separately headlined the arrest of the so-called "terror da Ajuda," a young offender convicted over a spree of violent street robberies in the area. These issues are tied to a specific residential pocket away from the Palácio da Ajuda/riverside tourist core, not the freguesia's main visitor sites.

text: Vale de Alcântara (Quinta do Loureiro, around Avenida de Ceuta) is a well-documented, recurring open-air drug trafficking and consumption site linked to the relocation of former Casal Ventoso residents. Diário de Notícias (13 Feb 2024) quoted a local parish leader saying "the drug problem has never been this bad" since 2017, describing hundreds of users, accumulated syringes and violence against both users and residents; the PSP ran repeated enforcement operations in 2025, including "Operação Portas Trancadas" (25 May 2025, 9 detained, traffickers barricading residential buildings) and a further pretrial-detention case (Observador, 25 May 2025). This is a serious, persistent problem rather than an isolated incident.

text: Belém's own parish president is on record calling it "one of Lisbon's safest areas," and no night-time crime pattern turned up in press searches. However, organised pickpocket rings targeting tourists near the monuments are documented: Notícias ao Minuto (8 Aug 2025) reported the pretrial detention of five pickpockets who used coordinated blocking tactics and a card-reader device to rob a tourist near Praça do Império/Padrão dos Descobrimentos, part of a broader pattern of "sophisticated" pickpocket gangs working the Belém monument area.

text: Documented concerns are limited and localised rather than widespread. Notícias ao Minuto (24 Nov 2022) reported a PSP patrol intercepting a street-robbery group on Rua Cintura do Porto in Estrela, with one suspect detained; separately, an Observador investigative piece on Lisbon's most problematic areas listed the Madragoa and Fonte Santa neighbourhoods (both within the Estrela freguesia) alongside the old industrial part of Alcântara as flagged zones raised by parish officials. No pattern of daytime tourist-relevant crime was found in current press coverage.
sources: Notícias ao Minuto, 24 Nov 2022 – "Suspeito de roubos na via pública detido na Estrela, em Lisboa"
Observador – "Insegurança em Lisboa ou mera perceção? Um raio-X aos pontos mais problemáticos da capital" (Madragoa, Fonte Santa flagged)

text: A documented wave of robberies hit local shops in autumn 2024 — SOL (14 Oct 2024) reported shopkeepers alarmed by the spree, and Correio da Manhã followed up noting the parish council said PSP had already arrested seven suspects (the area was also noted in press as "the bairro where [mayor] Carlos Moedas lives"). Separately, a January 2024 pharmacy robbery ended with the armed suspect barricading himself in a nearby building before being detained by PSP (Correio da Manhã/CNN Portugal/TVI, 4 Jan 2024). The neighbourhood's western edge also borders the Vale de Alcântara/Quinta do Loureiro drug-trafficking hotspot, with Campo de Ourique's own parish officials co-signing an open letter about it; a resident group called "Campo de Ourique Mais Seguro" reflects ongoing local safety concern.

text: Covers Bairro Alto and Príncipe Real. No specific daytime safety concerns are documented in current press coverage — by day the area is calm and largely residential/boutique. By night, Bairro Alto is a well-documented hotspot for alcohol-fuelled disorder and robbery: a 22-year-old was fatally struck with a bottle during a robbery attempt on English tourists there in October 2023, a gang of armed teenagers (aged 15-19) robbed victims in Bairro Alto and nearby Santos in June 2023, and a 2025 report described a 'wave' of robberies hitting restaurants and bars. Residents and shopkeepers have complained since at least 2021 about worsening nighttime crime, and the parish council says only 7 of 200 promised CCTV cameras had actually been installed.

text: Covers Avenida da Liberdade, Marquês de Pombal and Rato. By day, organised gangs of 'scouts' have been documented targeting the avenue's jewellers in coordinated luxury-watch robberies, and elderly residents report a rise in fraud and petty theft. By night, Correio da Manhã reported residents alarmed by assaults and open drug consumption along Avenida da Liberdade, Jornal de Notícias reported a new PSP police station being opened there specifically because local crime had worsened, and CM separately reported an armed robbery at a jewellery store on the avenue. Coverage points to real but moderate, non-recurring-violent concerns rather than an entrenched crime corridor.

text: Covers Baixa, Chiado, Alfama, Castelo, Mouraria and Martim Moniz. By day, the historic core is a long-running pickpocketing hotspot for tourists, with repeated reports of wallet-theft rings around Alfama's viewpoints, the Baixa grid and the trams, and PSP still making frequent arrests (six Romanian pickpockets detained in a single 24-hour period, July 2025). By night the picture is more serious: Rua do Benformoso and Rua da Amendoeira in Mouraria host an open-air drug market police describe as serving '50 to 60 customers an hour' from noon to 2am, and Martim Moniz has seen a stabbing brawl that injured seven people (January 2025), an alleged rape that alarmed residents, and a contested PSP crackdown operation.

text: Covers Graça and the Santa Apolónia area. No serious violent-crime coverage names São Vicente specifically; the parish council itself told a 2025 Observador special report that it believes the 'feeling of insecurity has increased more than actual criminality', citing only pickpocketing on trams and occasional distraction thefts at outdoor cafés. One dated incident stands out — 47 parked cars were vandalised in Graça in November 2024 — but this reads as an isolated dispute rather than a recurring pattern. The overall documented concern is limited and non-violent, so day is rated green and night a light yellow.

text: Covers Anjos, Intendente (Largo do Intendente Pina Manique) and the Avenida Almirante Reis corridor. By day, the parish council asked the city in February 2025 for CCTV cameras citing shop robberies, vehicle break-ins and a documented 5% rise in thefts (2023 vs 2022) concentrated in dense pedestrian streets. By night, Largo do Intendente carries a long, repeatedly documented history of open drug dealing and street prostitution stretching back over a decade, and residents described ongoing violence and insecurity there as recently as October 2023 despite years of municipal redevelopment efforts.

text: Real press coverage documents a serious violent incident: a triple homicide at a barbershop on Rua Henrique Barrilaro Ruas (2 Oct 2024, per Observador and Visão), after which neighbours left retaliation threats and two vehicles were torched the same night. A further homicide arrest was reported there in August 2026. Daytime coverage is more moderate, citing minor thefts and vehicle damage around Rua Morais Soares/Quinta do Lavrado linked to drug use, and a joint PSP firearms operation across Areeiro/Penha de França/Beato (Dec 2022).

text: Coverage repeatedly links Beato to drug trafficking: Diário de Notícias reported seven people caught in flagrante dealing drugs in Beato, and Jornal A Nação reported a separate trafficking arrest in the freguesia. An Observador special report notes the parish concentrates over 550 homeless people across shelters and that local leadership describes a considerably increased feeling of insecurity, especially between Xabregas and Beato, tied to trafficking and robberies rather than confirmed statistical crime increases. A joint PSP firearms sweep (Dec 2022) also covered Beato alongside Areeiro and Penha de França.

text: Marvila is the most heavily and repeatedly documented of the five for serious drug-related crime, largely centred on the Chelas public-housing area within it. Visão (3 Oct 2024) reported the conviction, to 19 years, of "Samir, rei do crack," leader of the so-called "grupo de Chelas"; Observador's special report described how PSP dismantled a group "controlled by terror" running one of Lisbon's busiest open-air drug points, earning about €3,000/day. Correio da Manhã separately reported Chelas youths threatening rivals with gun photos online, and JN reported an 11kg drug network dismantled in Chelas. PSP operations recur into 2025-2026: CNN Portugal covered a Marvila weapons/drugs cordon (Dec 2023), TVI/CNN reported four detained with drugs and guns seized in a Marvila bairro operation (21 Jan 2026), and TVI reported joint PSP searches of 12 homes across Olivais and Marvila (17 Dec 2025).

text: Coverage shows isolated but real incidents rather than a systemic pattern: a PSP weapons operation ("Laços de Pólvora," 29 Nov 2022) detained nine people and seized cash and firearms in an Olivais housing estate; a security guard was assaulted and doused with gasoline during an armed robbery at the Quinta Pedagógica dos Olivais (Oct 2022); and TVI reported a robbery victim in Olivais running over the assailant while trying to recover stolen property. Olivais was also swept in a joint Dec 2025 PSP operation with Marvila. Notably, the parish's own leadership told Observador it detects neither rising crime nor greater insecurity feeling and identified no specific hotspot, so this is rated moderate rather than serious.

text: Contrary to its upscale, purpose-built reputation, real press coverage does document property-crime concerns here, though not street violence affecting pedestrians by day. Correio da Manhã ran the headline "Assaltos afligem Parque das Nações" and separately reported a burglar couple caught on camera in the district. CNN Portugal (9 Feb 2024) reported a kidnapping, threats and robbery case in Parque das Nações resulting in two PSP arrests. High-value home burglaries (including a widely covered €500k cash-and-jewellery theft, Aug 2026) have also been reported in Lisbon's affluent districts, of which this is one. No daytime street-crime pattern was found in coverage, so day is rated green.

text: Local and national press have repeatedly documented a rise in break-ins and vandalism in Areeiro, alongside what one parish official called drug trafficking that is "evident to everyone," concentrated around the Portugal Novo social-housing area; the same official summarised it as "peace by day, war by night." PSP has run special operations in the parish (jointly with Penha de Franca and Beato) seizing drugs, arms and munitions, and separately detained a man for drugs/arms found during a traffic stop in Areeiro. Daytime problems (opportunistic theft, vandalism, aggressive begging) are documented but described as markedly less severe than after dark.

text: Coverage is more limited than in most neighbouring freguesias: a local outlet reported a spate of "violent assaults" alarming residents in September 2024, and a residents' petition circulated over a perceived rise in assaults; a residential burglary was intercepted by PSP one night in August 2023. In Lisbon's 2024/2025 parish-by-parish security survey, the Avenidas Novas junta did not respond, leaving official comment thin. No specific daytime safety concerns were found in current press coverage.

text: Reporting shows scattered but real armed-crime incidents rather than a chronic hotspot: a pawn-shop customer was robbed of a large quantity of gold in August 2026, a football fan was robbed at gunpoint near Estádio José Alvalade, and the stadium itself was robbed during a title-deciding match in May 2025. Lisbon's parish security survey flagged night-time concentration of students around Avenida do Brasil/Campo Grande as a concern warranting reinforced patrols (including mounted GNR), and separate reporting recorded a drug-trafficking arrest and preventive detention in the parish. No evidence of a chronic drug corridor or gang-territory problem was found.

text: Campolide has been repeatedly named in a documented wave of armed robberies: a "Rolex gang" has held victims up at gunpoint since 2025, continuing into January 2026, targeting people around Avenida da Liberdade, Amoreiras and Campolide; a shopkeeper was stabbed multiple times during an armed robbery of an electronics store in December 2025. In Lisbon's parish security survey, Campolide's own junta named simple theft, vehicle break-ins and drug-product trafficking as the most common problems locally, saying they create a "generalised sense of insecurity." Older reporting also documents long-standing neglect and marginality issues around the Bela Flor social-housing pocket.

text: Local press documented a recurring "wave of thefts" in early 2025, described by residents as happening "every week," including a shopkeeper assaulted and needing eight stitches; the parish president publicly requested reinforced PSP presence and video surveillance. PSP has separately made arrests over a string of violent robberies and a drug-trafficking case near the Sete Rios terminal, plus an ATM explosion and an armed robbery at a petrol station within the freguesia. Coverage is fairly consistent but describes property crime and isolated violent incidents rather than a chronic gang or open drug-dealing corridor.

text: The freguesia's own parish council (Junta de Freguesia de Benfica) publicly linked a rise in robberies to the area's transport links and proximity to Amadora, proposing security cameras at 26 locations in 2024. The Bairro da Boavista (within Benfica) saw a stabbing homicide between brothers, a stoned bus, and reinforced PSP policing in January 2025 after resident complaints of assaults, plus a Lisbon Municipal Assembly recommendation for more policing after a residents' petition. Daytime disturbances are more isolated (occasional Estádio da Luz matchday clashes between fans and police), while night-time robbery and unrest reports are more sustained and recent.

text: Carnide's Bairro Padre Cruz is a recurring, well-documented drug-dealing and violence hotspot: PSP recorded 21 arrests there in a single month (2023), and separate shooting incidents left four people wounded in 2020 and two more in 2022, both widely covered by Publico, Observador, DN and JN. A group also attacked the local police station and threatened further violence (Correio da Manhã), and PSP has run repeated raids there targeting jewellery-store robbery suspects. Given the frequency and severity of drug-trafficking operations and armed incidents, both day and night carry serious documented risk in this specific bairro, though other parts of the freguesia are not similarly flagged.

text: The Alta de Lisboa area within Lumiar has been the target of repeated PSP drug-trafficking crackdowns, including a major operation in November 2025 (jointly with neighbouring Ameixoeira) that seized weapons and made arrests, and an earlier network dismantled by PSP in 2013 described as the area's 'most active' trafficking group. Correio da Manhã also reported a shooting near a church in Alta de Lisboa and a separate daytime robbery/arrest in Lumiar. Documented incidents concentrate on drug-trafficking operations and isolated violent episodes rather than routine daytime street crime, so night-time risk is rated higher than day.

text: Santa Clara freguesia includes the Bairro da Ameixoeira, subject of a detailed Publico investigative report (April 2026) describing an entrenched, unresolved drug-dealing scene ('a droga não se resolve, gere-se'), plus a joint PSP mega-operation with neighbouring Alta de Lisboa in November 2025 that seized weapons and drugs and made arrests, and an earlier raid that detained 11 people and seized drugs and firearms (RTP/Sábado). No sources describing daytime street crime, pickpocketing or violent incidents against ordinary residents/tourists were found for Santa Clara specifically, so the concern documented is concentrated around organised drug trafficking rather than general street danger.
